tai.rule: る-verbs drop る and add たい.

potential.rule: る-verbs swap る for られる. In speech people often drop the ら: ～れる.

volitional.rule: る-verbs swap る for よう.

imperative.rule: る-verbs swap る for ろ.

prohibitive.rule: Add な to the dictionary form.

ba.rule: る-verbs swap る for れば.

tara.rule: Add ら to the plain past.

passive.rule: る-verbs swap る for られる (the same as the potential).

causative.rule: る-verbs swap る for させる.

caus_pass.rule: る-verbs swap る for させられる.

teiru.rule: Add いる to the て-form. In speech the い often drops: ～てる.

teshimau.rule: Add しまう to the て-form. In speech ～てしまう becomes ～ちゃう.

sou.rule: る-verbs drop る and add そう.

sugiru.rule: る-verbs drop る and add すぎる.

yasui.rule: る-verbs drop る and add やすい.

nikui.rule: る-verbs drop る and add にくい.

temo.rule: Take the て-form and add も.

tari.rule: Take the plain past and add り, usually in pairs: ～たり～たりする.

nagara.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add ながら.

zuni.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずに. する becomes せずに.

teoku.rule: Take the て-form and add おく. In speech ～ておく becomes ～とく (～でおく becomes ～どく).

tearu.rule: Take the て-form and add ある. Only for transitive verbs (ones that take を).

temiru.rule: Take the て-form and add みる.

potential_neg.rule: Start from the dictionary form → potential, then make it negative like a る-verb: 書ける → 書けない.

passive_past.rule: Start from the dictionary form → passive, then past like a る-verb: 書かれる → 書かれた.

caus_past.rule: Start from the dictionary form → causative, then past like a る-verb: 書かせる → 書かせた.

volitional_to.rule: Take the volitional (書こう, 食べよう, しよう) and add とする.

ba_hodo.rule: Start from the dictionary form → the ば form, then the dictionary form again, then ほど: 書けば書くほど.

rashii.rule: Take the dictionary form and add らしい.

youda.rule: Take the dictionary form and add ようだ (or みたい in speech).

hazu.rule: Take the dictionary form and add はずだ.

sasete_itadaku.rule: Causative て-form + いただきます: 書かせていただきます (let me write).

zaruwoenai.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ざるを得ない. する becomes せざるを得ない.

zuniwairarenai.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずにはいられない. する becomes せずにはいられない.

あずけらずにはいられない

kaneru.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add かねる.

kanenai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add かねない.

uru.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add 得る, read うる or える.

ppanashi.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add っぱなし.

gachi.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add がち.

kkonai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add っこない.

youganai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add ようがない.

gatai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add がたい (難い).

beki.rule: Take the dictionary form and add べき (べきだ at the end of a sentence). する also gives すべき.

mai.rule: Take the dictionary form and add まい. る-verbs can also drop る (食べまい); する gives するまい or すまい, 来る gives 来るまい or 来(こ)まい.

nu.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ぬ (or ん). する becomes せぬ.

neba.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ねばならない. する becomes せねばならない.
m: あずけらねばならない

zutomo.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずとも. する becomes せずとも.

nbakari.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add んばかり. する becomes せんばかり.

beku.rule: Take the dictionary form and add べく. する usually gives すべく.

nganame.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add んがため. する becomes せんがため.

you_mononara.rule: Take the volitional (書こう, 食べよう, しよう) and add ものなら.

masu.rule: う-verbs change the final う to い, then add ます.

masu_neg.rule: Use the ます-stem (い for the final う) and add ません.

masu_past.rule: Use the ます-stem (い for the final う) and add ました.

masu_past_neg.rule: Use the ます-stem (い for the final う) and add ませんでした.

masho.rule: Use the ます-stem (い for the final う) and add ましょう.

dict.rule: Take off ます and change the い-row kana back to its う-row kana. る-verbs just swap ます for る.

nai.rule: う-verbs change the final う to わ, then add ない. Verbs ending in う use わ, not あ.

rashii.rule: Take the dictionary form and add らしい.

youda.rule: Take the dictionary form and add ようだ (or みたい in speech).

hazu.rule: Take the dictionary form and add はずだ.

sasete_itadaku.rule: Causative て-form + いただきます: 書かせていただきます (let me write).

zaruwoenai.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ざるを得ない. する becomes せざるを得ない.

zuniwairarenai.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずにはいられない. する becomes せずにはいられない.

kaneru.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add かねる.

kanenai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add かねない.

uru.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add 得る, read うる or える.

ppanashi.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add っぱなし.

gachi.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add がち.

kkonai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add っこない.

youganai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add ようがない.

gatai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add がたい (難い).

beki.rule: Take the dictionary form and add べき (べきだ at the end of a sentence). する also gives すべき.

mai.rule: Take the dictionary form and add まい. る-verbs can also drop る (食べまい); する gives するまい or すまい, 来る gives 来るまい or 来(こ)まい.

nu.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ぬ (or ん). する becomes せぬ.

neba.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ねばならない. する becomes せねばならない.

zutomo.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずとも. する becomes せずとも.

nbakari.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add んばかり. する becomes せんばかり.

beku.rule: Take the dictionary form and add べく. する usually gives すべく.

nganame.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add んがため. する becomes せんがため.

you_mononara.rule: Take the volitional (書こう, 食べよう, しよう) and add ものなら.

potential.rule: る-verbs swap る for られる. In speech people often drop the ら: ～れる.

volitional.rule: る-verbs swap る for よう.

imperative.rule: る-verbs swap る for ろ.

prohibitive.rule: Add な to the dictionary form.

ba.rule: る-verbs swap る for れば.

tara.rule: Add ら to the plain past.

passive.rule: る-verbs swap る for られる (the same as the potential).

causative.rule: る-verbs swap る for させる.

caus_pass.rule: る-verbs swap る for させられる.

teiru.rule: Add いる to the て-form. In speech the い often drops: ～てる.

teshimau.rule: Add しまう to the て-form. In speech ～てしまう becomes ～ちゃう.

sou.rule: る-verbs drop る and add そう.

sugiru.rule: る-verbs drop る and add すぎる.

yasui.rule: る-verbs drop る and add やすい.

nikui.rule: る-verbs drop る and add にくい.

temo.rule: Take the て-form and add も.

tari.rule: Take the plain past and add り, usually in pairs: ～たり～たりする.

nagara.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add ながら.

zuni.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずに. する becomes せずに.

teoku.rule: Take the て-form and add おく. In speech ～ておく becomes ～とく (～でおく becomes ～どく).

tearu.rule: Take the て-form and add ある. Only for transitive verbs (ones that take を).

temiru.rule: Take the て-form and add みる.

potential_neg.rule: Start from the dictionary form → potential, then make it negative like a る-verb: 書ける → 書けない.

passive_past.rule: Start from the dictionary form → passive, then past like a る-verb: 書かれる → 書かれた.

caus_past.rule: Start from the dictionary form → causative, then past like a る-verb: 書かせる → 書かせた.

volitional_to.rule: Take the volitional (書こう, 食べよう, しよう) and add とする.

ba_hodo.rule: Start from the dictionary form → the ば form, then the dictionary form again, then ほど: 書けば書くほど.

rashii.rule: Take the dictionary form and add らしい.

youda.rule: Take the dictionary form and add ようだ (or みたい in speech).

hazu.rule: Take the dictionary form and add はずだ.

nai.rule: う-verbs change the final く to か, then add ない.

ta.rule: The plain past is the て-form with た for て (だ for で): く becomes いた.

te.rule: In the て-form, く becomes いて.

prohibitive.rule: Add な to the dictionary form.

ba.rule: う-verbs change the final く to け, then add ば.

tara.rule: Add ら to the plain past.

passive.rule: う-verbs change the final く to か, then add れる.

causative.rule: う-verbs change the final く to か, then add せる.

caus_pass.rule: う-verbs change the final く to か, then add される (or せられる).

teiru.rule: Add いる to the て-form. In speech the い often drops: ～てる.

teshimau.rule: Add しまう to the て-form. In speech ～てしまう becomes ～ちゃう (～でしまう becomes ～じゃう).

sou.rule: Use the ます-stem (き for the final く) and add そう.

sugiru.rule: Use the ます-stem (き for the final く) and add すぎる.

yasui.rule: Use the ます-stem (き for the final く) and add やすい.

nikui.rule: Use the ます-stem (き for the final く) and add にくい.

zuni.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずに. する becomes せずに.

teoku.rule: Take the て-form and add おく. In speech ～ておく becomes ～とく (～でおく becomes ～どく).

tearu.rule: Take the て-form and add ある. Only for transitive verbs (ones that take を).

temiru.rule: Take the て-form and add みる.

potential_neg.rule: Start from the dictionary form → potential, then make it negative like a る-verb: 書ける → 書けない.

passive_past.rule: Start from the dictionary form → passive, then past like a る-verb: 書かれる → 書かれた.

caus_past.rule: Start from the dictionary form → causative, then past like a る-verb: 書かせる → 書かせた.

volitional_to.rule: Take the volitional (書こう, 食べよう, しよう) and add とする.

ba_hodo.rule: Start from the dictionary form → the ば form, then the dictionary form again, then ほど: 書けば書くほど.

rashii.rule: Take the dictionary form and add らしい.

youda.rule: Take the dictionary form and add ようだ (or みたい in speech).

hazu.rule: Take the dictionary form and add はずだ.

sasete_itadaku.rule: Causative て-form + いただきます: 書かせていただきます (let me write).

zaruwoenai.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ざるを得ない. する becomes せざるを得ない.

zuniwairarenai.rule: Take the old negative stem (書か, 食べ, せ for する, 来(こ) for 来る) and add ずにはいられない. する becomes せずにはいられない.

kanenai.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add かねない.

uru.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add 得る, read うる or える.

ppanashi.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add っぱなし.

gachi.rule: Take the ます-stem (書き, 食べ, し, 来(き)) and add がち.

blocks.s: Every verb belongs to one of three groups, and the group decides how it conjugates. Get the group right and the rest follows.
**る-verbs** (ichidan) end in **-iる** or **-eる**: 食べる (たべる), 見る (みる), 起きる (おきる). To conjugate them you drop る and add the ending.
**う-verbs** (godan) are everything else: verbs ending in う, く, ぐ, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む, or る after an a, u or o sound, like 書く, 飲む and 分かる. Their last kana moves through the あ-い-う-え-お row.
**Irregular verbs** are just する and 来る (くる), plus every verb made with する, like 勉強する.

The trap: some verbs end in -iる or -eる but are う-verbs anyway. The common ones are 帰る (かえる), 入る (はいる), 知る (しる), 走る (はしる), 要る (いる) and 切る (きる). You can't tell from the spelling, so learn them as a list.
The ます form is the polite present: what you say to people you don't know well. It's built on the **ます-stem**.
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its い-row partner, then add ます. 書く → 書き → 書きます. 飲む → 飲みます. 話す → 話します. 待つ → 待ちます.
**る-verbs:** drop る and add ます. 食べる → 食べます. 見る → 見ます.
**Irregular:** する → します, 来る → 来ます (きます).
For the negative, swap ます for **ません**: 書きません, 食べません, しません.

sections.title: The ます form: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I get up at six every morning.
I don't drink alcohol.
A friend is coming to my house.

blocks.s: The past of ます is **ました**, and the past of ません is **ませんでした**. Both build on the same ます-stem.
行く → 行きました, 行きませんでした. 寝る → 寝ました, 寝ませんでした.
**ましょう** means "let's": 行きましょう (let's go). With a question, ましょうか offers to do something: 持ちましょうか (shall I carry it?).
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Yesterday I went to a film with a friend.
I didn't sleep much last night.
It's late, so let's go home.
I studied at the library at the weekend.

blocks.s: Dictionaries list verbs in their **dictionary form**, and the plain forms you'll learn next all start from it. So you need to get from the ます form back to it.
**う-verbs:** take off ます and change the い-row kana to its う-row partner. 読みます → 読み → 読む. 作ります → 作る. 洗います → 洗う.
**る-verbs:** take off ます and add る. 借ります → 借りる. 教えます → 教える.
**Irregular:** します → する, 来ます → 来る (くる).
This is where the う-verb traps catch people: 入ります comes from 入る (はいる), not 入りる. If the ます-stem ends in an い-row kana other than the る-verb's own vowel, it's a う-verb.

sections.title: Back to the dictionary form: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I like reading before bed.
I can cook.
I brush my teeth before getting in the bath.

blocks.s: With friends and family, and inside longer sentences, Japanese uses the **plain** forms. The plain negative ends in **ない**.
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **あ-row** partner, then add ない. 書く → 書かない. 飲む → 飲まない. 待つ → 待たない.
Verbs ending in **う** use **わ**, not あ: 買う → 買わない, 会う → 会わない.
**る-verbs:** drop る and add ない. 食べる → 食べない.
**Irregular:** する → しない, 来る → 来ない (こない). Note the reading change.
ある is the odd one out: its negative is just **ない**. Never あらない.

sections.title: The plain negative (ない): in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I never eat breakfast.
I don't have time today.
He still hasn't come.

blocks.s: The **て-form** joins verbs together, makes requests (～てください) and builds many later forms. It's the most important form to get automatic.
**る-verbs:** drop る and add て. 食べる → 食べて. 見る → 見て.
**Irregular:** する → して, 来る → 来て (きて).
**う-verbs** depend on their last kana. This lesson covers three of the groups:
く → **いて**: 書く → 書いて, 聞く → 聞いて.
ぐ → **いで**: 泳ぐ → 泳いで.
す → **して**: 話す → 話して, 貸す → 貸して.
行く is the one exception: 行って, not 行いて.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Please write your name here.
I went to the station and got on a train.
When I get up in the morning I take a shower straight away.

blocks.s: The other two groups of う-verbs:
う, つ, る → **って**: 買う → 買って, 待つ → 待って, 帰る → 帰って.
む, ぶ, ぬ → **んで**: 飲む → 飲んで, 遊ぶ → 遊んで, 死ぬ → 死んで.
A rhyme some learners use: "う-つ-る って, む-ぶ-ぬ んで, く いて, ぐ いで, す して". Remember the る here means う-verbs ending in る, like 帰る and 乗る. る-verbs just take て.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Please wait a moment.
Please try reading this book.
I went home and made dinner.
The children are playing in the park.

blocks.s: Once you know the て-form, the plain past is free: swap て for **た** (and で for **だ**). 書いて → 書いた. 飲んで → 飲んだ. 食べて → 食べた. 行って → 行った.
The plain past negative takes the ない form and swaps ない for **なかった**. 書かない → 書かなかった. 来ない → 来なかった (こなかった). ない → なかった.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Yesterday I ate sushi for the first time.
It rained, so I didn't go anywhere.
I spoke to the teacher in Japanese.
There didn't use to be a convenience store here.

lessons.title: Wanting, and asking someone not to

sections.title: Wanting, and asking someone not to

blocks.s: **たい** means "want to". Add it to the ます-stem: 食べる → 食べたい, 行く → 行きたい, する → したい. It then conjugates like an い-adjective: 食べたくない, 食べたかった.
**ないで** is the negative て-form. Add で to the ない form: 忘れない → 忘れないで. With ください it asks someone not to do something: 忘れないでください (please don't forget).

sections.title: Wanting, and asking someone not to: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I want to go to Hokkaido in the summer holidays.
Please don't forget about tomorrow.
I'm tired, so I want to rest a little.
Please don't come tomorrow.

blocks.s: This lesson mixes every verb form so far, with new words. Take your time on the て-form groups and the う-verbs that look like る-verbs.

cards.en: I bought bread near the station.
Please call a taxi.
I don't understand what this word means.
It snowed yesterday.
I don't smoke.
Someday I want to live in Kyoto.

blocks.s: Japanese has two kinds of adjective, and they conjugate differently.
**い-adjectives** end in い and change that い: 高い, 新しい, 寒い. They can go straight before a noun: 高い山.
**な-adjectives** don't conjugate themselves; they take だ, です, な and so on, just like nouns: 静か, 有名, 便利. Before a noun they need な: 静かな部屋.
The traps are な-adjectives that end in い: **きれい** and **嫌い** (きらい). They look like い-adjectives, but you say きれいな部屋 and きれいじゃない. Learn them as exceptions.
The negative swaps the final い for **くない**: 高い → 高くない. 新しい → 新しくない.
To be polite, add **です**: 高いです, 高くないです. くありません is a more formal polite negative: 高くありません.
**いい** is irregular. In everything except its present form it becomes よい: いい → **よくない**, not いくない.

sections.title: い-adjectives in the present: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: It's not very cold today, is it.
This restaurant isn't expensive.
The weather isn't good, so I'm staying in.

blocks.s: The past swaps い for **かった**: 楽しい → 楽しかった. Its negative swaps い for **くなかった**: 楽しくなかった.
For polite, add です: 楽しかったです, 楽しくなかったです. Never 楽しいでした: the past belongs to the adjective, not to です.
いい → よかった, よくなかった. "よかったです" is a very common reply: "that's good" or "I'm glad".

sections.title: い-adjectives in the past: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: The trip was really fun.
The test wasn't as hard as I'd thought.
Last summer was really hot.
You passed the exam, that's great.

lessons.title: な-adjectives and nouns in the present

sections.title: な-adjectives and nouns in the present

blocks.s: な-adjectives and nouns conjugate the same way, by changing the word after them.
Plain: **だ** (静かだ, 学生だ). Negative: **じゃない** (静かじゃない). ではない is more formal and also right.
Polite: **です** (静かです). Negative: **じゃありません** (or ではありません, じゃないです).
In everyday speech the plain だ is often left off, especially by women and in questions, but your answers here should include it.

sections.title: な-adjectives and nouns in the present: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I don't like spicy food.
This shop is famous for its ramen.
My older brother isn't a student any more.

lessons.title: な-adjectives and nouns in the past

sections.title: な-adjectives and nouns in the past

blocks.s: The past is **だった**, and **でした** to be polite: 元気だった, 元気でした.
The past negative is **じゃなかった**, and **じゃありませんでした** (or じゃなかったです) to be polite.

sections.title: な-adjectives and nouns in the past: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Work was closed yesterday.
I was busy last week and had no free time at all.
The autumn leaves in Kyoto were beautiful.
I was often ill as a child.

blocks.s: **Before a noun:** い-adjectives stay as they are (高い山). な-adjectives take **な** (静かな部屋). Nouns take **の** (学生の時).
**Adverbs** describe how something is done. い-adjectives swap い for **く**: 早い → 早く (早く起きる, get up early). な-adjectives take **に**: 上手 → 上手に (上手に話す, speak well).
いい becomes よく: よく分かる (understand well).

sections.title: Before a noun, and adverbs: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I'd prefer a quieter room.
I'm getting up early tomorrow.
I cleaned the room nicely.
I lived in Tokyo when I was a student.

blocks.s: To join an adjective or noun to what follows ("cheap and tasty", "a student and…"), use its て-form.
い-adjectives swap い for **くて**: 安い → 安くて. いい → よくて.
な-adjectives and nouns take **で**: 静かで, 学生で.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: This place is cheap and tasty.
It's near the station and convenient: a good flat.
It's raining today, and cold.

blocks.s: Every adjective and noun form so far, with new words. Watch for きれい and 嫌い, and for いい turning into よ.

cards.en: Hokkaido was very cold.
My leg hurts, and it's not really OK.
This is a precious watch my mother gave me.
Please be quiet in the library.
As a child I didn't dislike vegetables.
This room is small and dark.

blocks.s: The potential says you **can** do something.
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **え-row** partner and add る. 書く → 書ける. 泳ぐ → 泳げる. 待つ → 待てる. The result is a る-verb: 書けない, 書けます.
**る-verbs:** swap る for **られる**. 食べる → 食べられる. In speech the ら often drops (食べれる); both count here.
**Irregular:** する → **できる**. 来る → 来られる (こられる), or 来れる in speech.
With the potential, the object often takes が instead of を: 日本語**が**話せます.

sections.title: Can do: the potential: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I've been able to swim since I was a child.
I can speak a little Japanese.
Can you come to the party tomorrow?
I'm looking for someone who can drive.

blocks.s: The plain volitional is the casual "let's" (行こう!) and also "I'll" or "shall I" when thinking aloud. With と思う it means "I'm thinking of doing": 行こうと思う.
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **お-row** partner and add う. 行く → 行こう. 飲む → 飲もう. 帰る → 帰ろう.
**る-verbs:** swap る for **よう**. 食べる → 食べよう.
**Irregular:** する → しよう, 来る → 来よう (こよう).
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Let's go together.
Let's do our best tomorrow too!
The weather's nice, so I'm thinking of going for a walk in the park.

blocks.s: The **imperative** is a blunt command. You'll mostly see it on signs, in sport and in anger, so use ～てください in real life.
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **え-row** partner. 書く → 書け. 走る → 走れ. 止まる → 止まれ (the word on stop signs).
**る-verbs:** swap る for **ろ**. 食べる → 食べろ. 逃げる → 逃げろ.
**Irregular:** する → しろ (せよ in writing), 来る → 来い (こい).
The **prohibitive** is a blunt "don't": just add **な** to the dictionary form. 入る → 入るな (no entry).
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Danger! Run!
Don't go into this room.
Run faster!

blocks.s: **ば** means "if". It focuses on the condition itself: "if you do X, Y follows".
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **え-row** partner and add ば. 行く → 行けば. 待つ → 待てば.
**る-verbs:** swap る for **れば**. 食べる → 食べれば.
**Irregular:** する → すれば, 来る → 来れば (くれば). ある → あれば.
**い-adjectives:** swap い for **ければ**: 安い → 安ければ. いい → よければ.
**な-adjectives and nouns:** add **なら** (or であれば): 静かなら, 雨なら.

sections.title: If: the ば conditional: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: If you read this book, you'll understand.
If you like, shall we go together?
If I had the money, I'd like to buy a car.
If it rains, the match is off.

lessons.title: If and when: the たら conditional

sections.title: If and when: the たら conditional

blocks.s: **たら** is the most flexible "if", and also "when" for things that will definitely happen. Add **ら** to the plain past: 着いた → 着いたら. 見た → 見たら.
For adjectives and nouns, also add ら to the past: 暑かった → 暑かったら, 暇だった → 暇だったら.
駅に着いたら電話してください means "call me when you get to the station". ば can't be used for that.

sections.title: If and when: the たら conditional: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Call me when you get to the station.
Let's go for a drink when work's over.
If you're free, could you help me?
If you're hot, you can open the window.

lessons.title: ている and てしまう

sections.title: ている and てしまう

blocks.s: **ている** (て-form + いる) describes something going on now (雨が降っている, it's raining) or a state that continues (結婚している, be married; 知っている, know). In speech the い drops: 降ってる.
**てしまう** (て-form + しまう) means doing something completely, or something happening that you regret: 財布をなくしてしまった (I've gone and lost my wallet). In speech it shrinks: ～てしまう → **～ちゃう**, ～でしまう → **～じゃう**.

sections.title: ている and てしまう: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: It's raining outside.
My older sister lives in Osaka.
My little brother always ends up eating all the cake.
I often leave my homework at home by mistake.

blocks.s: The **passive** says something is done to someone: "I was praised", "my foot was stepped on". Often it carries a feeling of being troubled by it.
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **あ-row** partner and add れる. 書く → 書かれる. 踏む → 踏まれる. 言う → 言われる (わ, as in the ない form).
**る-verbs:** swap る for **られる**. 食べる → 食べられる. Yes, that's the same as the potential: the sentence tells you which.
**Irregular:** する → される, 来る → 来られる (こられる).
The person doing it takes に: 先生**に**褒められた (I was praised by the teacher).
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Bikes often get stolen in this town.
I'm happy when the teacher praises me.
On crowded trains, people often step on your feet.
It's a nuisance when friends turn up late at night.

blocks.s: The **causative** means making or letting someone do something. Which one depends on the context: 子供に野菜を食べさせる (make the children eat vegetables), 好きなだけ遊ばせる (let them play as much as they like).
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **あ-row** partner and add せる. 書く → 書かせる. 飲む → 飲ませる. 習う → 習わせる.
**る-verbs:** swap る for **させる**. 食べる → 食べさせる.
**Irregular:** する → させる, 来る → 来させる (こさせる).
～させてください is a polite way to ask to do something yourself: 私にやらせてください (please let me do it).

sections.title: Make and let: the causative: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: My mother makes me eat vegetables.
It's not good to keep friends waiting a long time.
I'm planning to have my child learn the piano.

blocks.s: The **causative-passive** means being made to do something, usually against your will: 飲まされた (I was made to drink).
**う-verbs:** change the last kana to its **あ-row** partner and add **される**: 飲む → 飲まされる. The longer ～せられる (飲ませられる) is also correct. Verbs ending in す can only take the long form: 話す → 話させられる.
**る-verbs:** swap る for **させられる**. 食べる → 食べさせられる.
**Irregular:** する → させられる, 来る → 来させられる (こさせられる).

sections.title: Made to: the causative-passive: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: At work parties I always get made to drink.
You always get kept waiting a long time at that hospital.
Whenever we go to karaoke, I get made to sing.

blocks.s: **そう** after a verb's ます-stem means something looks about to happen: 雨が降りそう (it looks like rain). After an adjective it means "looks": い-adjectives swap い for そう (高そう), な-adjectives just add it (元気そう).
いい becomes **よさそう**. And そう never goes on colour adjectives or かわいい: you can see they're red or cute, so there's nothing to guess.
**すぎる** means "too much". Add it to a verb's ます-stem (食べすぎる, eat too much), to an い-adjective without い (高すぎる), or to a な-adjective (静かすぎる). It's a る-verb: 食べすぎた.

sections.title: Looks like, and too much: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: The sky's dark; it looks like rain.
If you drink too much, the next day is hard.
This cake looks delicious.
This bag is too expensive for me.

lessons.title: Easy to, hard to, and becoming

sections.title: Easy to, hard to, and becoming

blocks.s: **やすい** and **にくい** go on a verb's ます-stem: 読みやすい (easy to read), 分かりにくい (hard to understand). The result is an い-adjective.
**なる** means "become". い-adjectives swap い for **く**: 寒くなる (get cold). な-adjectives and nouns take **に**: 静かになる, 医者になる.

sections.title: Easy to, hard to, and becoming: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: This pen is really easy to use.
The teacher's explanation is a bit hard to understand.
If you practise every day, you'll definitely get good.
Once it's November, it suddenly gets cold.

blocks.s: Every N4 form, with new words. The potential and passive of る-verbs look the same; let the sentence tell you which.

cards.en: I've become able to read a few kanji.
Please wait here until your name is called.
If you hurry, you'll make it.
Do you know that person's name?
On Sundays I let the children play in the park.
In the dorm we get made to clean the toilets every week.

blocks.s: **Respectful language** (尊敬語) raises the person doing something: a customer, your boss, a teacher. You use it for **their** actions, never your own.
The commonest verbs have their own respectful words:
行く, 来る, いる → **いらっしゃる**. 食べる, 飲む → **召し上がる** (めしあがる). 言う → **おっしゃる**. する → **なさる**. 見る → **ご覧になる** (ごらんになる). くれる → **くださる**. 着る → **お召しになる**.
"Please eat" to a guest is 召し上がってください. "Please come in" is いらっしゃい or いらっしゃいませ.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: What time is the company president coming?
I wonder what the president will have for lunch.
I understood what the teacher said.

blocks.s: **Humble language** (謙譲語) lowers yourself (or your company, or your family) when you act towards someone you respect. You use it for **your own** actions.

行く, 来る → **参る** (まいる). 行く (to visit someone) and 聞く → **伺う** (うかがう). いる → **おる**. 食べる, 飲む, もらう → **いただく**. 言う → **申す** (もうす), or 申し上げる. する → **いたす**. 見る → **拝見する** (はいけんする). 会う → **お目にかかる**. あげる → **差し上げる** (さしあげる).
Answers that match any of a word's humble verbs count as right: 行く can be 参る or 伺う.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

before: はじめまして。スミスと
cards.en: How do you do. My name is Smith.
I'll take a look at the materials later.
It's the first time I've received a gift from the president.

blocks.s: Verbs without a special keigo word use a pattern built on the ます-stem.
**Respectful:** **お + ます-stem + になる**. 書く → お書きになる. 待つ → お待ちになる. 帰る → お帰りになる.
**Humble:** **お + ます-stem + する**. 持つ → お持ちする (I'll carry it for you). 待つ → お待ちする.
する-verbs made from Chinese-origin words usually take **ご** instead of お: 説明する → ご説明になる, ご説明する. 連絡する → ご連絡する.
The pattern doesn't work for verbs whose ます-stem is a single kana, like 見る (見) or 寝る (寝). They use special words instead.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Until what time will the president wait?
I'll carry your luggage for you.
I'm planning to contact you tomorrow.

lessons.title: Keigo in the ます form

sections.title: Keigo in the ます form

blocks.s: In real conversations keigo verbs nearly always come in the **ます** form.
Most work like any other verb: 召し上がる → 召し上がります, 参る → 参ります, 拝見する → 拝見します.
**いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる** and **くださる** are special: their ます-stem ends in **い**, not り. いらっしゃいます, おっしゃいます, なさいます, くださいます.

sections.title: Keigo in the ます form: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Mr Tanaka is in the meeting room now.
I'll come to you tomorrow.
I'll show you the way.
The teacher always says so.

blocks.s: Respectful and humble verbs, special and regular, in dictionary and ます forms.

cards.en: The customer has arrived.
I'm looking forward to meeting the company president.
I'll be in the office all day tomorrow.
The president reads the newspaper every morning.

blocks.s: From here on, most "forms" are patterns built on forms you already know. Each lesson shows which form to start from.
**Must:** the ない form, swapping ない for **なければならない**: 書かない → 書かなければならない. なければいけない means the same. In speech it shrinks to **～なきゃ(いけない)**, **～なくちゃ(いけない)** or **～ないといけない**; all count here.
**Don't have to:** swap ない for **なくてもいい**: 書かなくてもいい.
**May:** the て-form plus **もいい**: 書いてもいい. Ask with か: 書いてもいいですか.
**Must not:** the て-form plus **はいけない**: 書いてはいけない. In speech ～ては becomes **～ちゃ**: 書いちゃいけない.

sections.title: Must, mustn't and may: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I have to get up at six tomorrow.
You mustn't smoke here.
May I use this room?
You don't have to come tomorrow.

options: don't have to (なくてもいい)

blocks.s: **Even if:** the て-form plus **も**: 行っても (even if I go). With いくら or どんなに it means "however much": いくら謝っても (however much I apologise).
Adjectives and nouns do the same: い-adjectives swap い for **くても** (高くても), な-adjectives and nouns take **でも** (静かでも, 雨でも).
**Things like:** the plain past plus **り**, usually in a pair ending with する: 本を読んだり、映画を見たりする (I do things like reading books and watching films).

sections.title: Even if, and things like: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

after: してくれませんでした。
cards.en: However much I apologised, they wouldn't forgive me.
Even if it rains, the match is on.
At weekends I read books, watch films and so on.
I want to buy it even if it's expensive.

blocks.s: **While:** the ます-stem plus **ながら**: 聞きながら (while listening). The main action comes last: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する (study while listening to music).
**Without:** the old negative stem plus **ずに**: 食べずに (without eating). It's the written cousin of ～ないで. する becomes **せずに**, and 来る becomes **来ずに** (こずに).
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I study while listening to music.
I went out without eating breakfast.
The day ended without my doing anything.
Looking at your phone while walking is dangerous.

lessons.title: In advance, already done, and trying

sections.title: In advance, already done, and trying

blocks.s: **Do in advance:** the て-form plus **おく**: 買っておく (buy it beforehand, so it's ready). In speech ～ておく becomes **～とく** (～でおく becomes ～どく): 買っとく.
**Has been done:** the て-form plus **ある** describes a state someone set up on purpose: 名前が書いてある (a name has been written). It only works with transitive verbs, ones that take を.
**Try doing:** the て-form plus **みる**: 読んでみる (read it and see).

sections.title: In advance, already done, and trying: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I'll get the drinks in before the party.
A name is written on the blackboard.
I'm going to try reading this book.
The key has been left on the desk.

blocks.s: N4 forms combine with the tenses you know. The potential, passive and causative all conjugate like る-verbs:
**Can't:** 書ける → 書け**ない**. 食べられる → 食べられ**ない** (or 食べれない).
**Was done:** 書かれる → 書かれ**た**.
**Made / let do:** 書かせる → 書かせ**た**.

sections.title: Couldn't, was done, made to: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I'm busy tomorrow and can't come.
This book was written a hundred years ago.
The mother made the child eat vegetables.
I can't read this kanji.

blocks.s: **Try to / be about to:** the volitional plus **とする**: 寝ようとする (try to sleep, be about to sleep).
**The more…, the more:** the ば form, then the dictionary form again, then **ほど**: 考えれば考えるほど (the more I think about it). For する-verbs, 勉強すればするほど is the usual shortening.
Adjectives too: 安ければ安いほど (the cheaper the better), 静かなら静かなほど.

sections.title: Trying to, and the more…: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Just as I was trying to get to sleep, the phone rang.
The more I think about it, the less I understand.
With vegetables, the cheaper the better.
Just as I was about to leave the house, it started to rain.

options: don't have to (なくてもいい)

blocks.s: **Apparently (らしい):** what you've heard. Add らしい to the plain form: 来るらしい. な-adjectives and nouns add it straight on: 静からしい, 病気らしい.
**It seems (ようだ / みたい):** your own impression. Add ようだ to the plain form: 降るようだ. な-adjectives take **なようだ**, nouns **のようだ**. In speech **みたい** replaces ようだ and joins straight on: 静かみたい.

sections.title: Apparently, and it seems: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Apparently a typhoon's coming tomorrow.
It looks like it'll snow tomorrow.
The teacher seems to be ill.
Apparently my brother's been very busy lately.

blocks.s: **はずだ** says what you expect from what you know: 着くはずだ (it should arrive). Add it to the plain form. な-adjectives take **なはずだ**, nouns **のはずだ**.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: The parcel should arrive tomorrow.
He should know about it too.
It should be quiet at night.
That person should still be a student.

lessons.title: Nouns from adjectives, and other people's feelings

sections.title: Nouns from adjectives, and other people's feelings

blocks.s: **さ** turns an adjective into a noun: 高い → **高さ** (height), 優しい → 優しさ (kindness), 大切 → 大切さ (importance). いい becomes よさ.

**がる** describes someone else's feelings, since in Japanese you can't state another person's feelings directly. Feeling adjectives swap い for がる: 欲しい → **欲しがる** (shows they want it), 寂しい → 寂しがる. It's a う-verb: 欲しがっている.

sections.title: Nouns from adjectives, and other people's feelings: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: This mountain is three thousand metres high.
Kids always want the latest games.
When Mum goes out, my little sister soon gets lonely.
I came to understand how precious family is.

blocks.s: **Please (お～ください):** お + ます-stem + ください, the polite way to ask a customer or guest: お待ちください. する-verbs from Chinese words take ご: ご説明ください. Some verbs have their own: 見る → **ご覧ください**, 来る → **お越しください**, 食べる → **召し上がってください**.
**Humble offers (お～いたします):** お + ます-stem + いたします, humbler than お～します: お持ちいたします (I'll carry it for you).
**Let me (させていただきます):** the causative て-form plus いただきます, literally "receive the favour of being allowed to": 説明させていただきます (allow me to explain).

sections.title: Polite requests and offers: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Please wait a moment.
Please come again any time.
I'll send you the materials tomorrow.
Then allow me to explain.

options: let me (させていただきます)
let me (させていただきます)
let me (させていただきます)

blocks.s: Every N3 pattern, with N3 words. For each, think about which form it builds on: the ない form, the て-form, the ます-stem or the plain form.

cards.en: I have to pay the rent by the end of this month.

lessons.title: No choice, and can't help it

sections.title: No choice, and can't help it

blocks.s: **Have no choice but to:** the old negative stem plus **ざるを得ない** (ざるをえない): 諦めざるを得ない. する becomes **せざるを得ない**.
**Can't help doing:** the old negative stem plus **ずにはいられない**: 笑わずにはいられない (I can't help laughing). する becomes せずにはいられない.
The old negative stem is the ない form without ない, except する uses **せ**: 書か, 食べ, せ, 来(こ).

sections.title: No choice, and can't help it: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: The rain was so bad we had to give up on the trip.
When I hear his stories, I can't help laughing.
If there's proof, I have to admit it.
I can't help saying this one thing.

lessons.title: Can't quite, might well, and could

sections.title: Can't quite, might well, and could

blocks.s: These three all go on the ます-stem.
**かねる** is a polite way to say you can't: 答えかねる (I'm unable to answer). You'll hear it in shops and offices: 分かりかねます.
**かねない** means something bad might well happen: 言いかねない (he might well say it).
**得る** (read うる or える) means something is possible: 考え得る (conceivable). Its negative is always 得ない (えない).

sections.title: Can't quite, might well, and could: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I'm afraid I can't answer that question.
He might well say something like that.
That's quite conceivable.
At this rate I might well forget an important appointment.

lessons.title: Left as is, and tends to

sections.title: Left as is, and tends to

blocks.s: **っぱなし** on the ます-stem means something was left in a state that should have been dealt with: 開けっぱなし (left open).
**がち** on the ます-stem means something tends to happen, usually something bad: 忘れがち (forgetful), 遅れがち. It works like a な-adjective: 忘れがちな人, 忘れがちになる. Some nouns take it too: 病気がち.

sections.title: Left as is, and tends to: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I fell asleep with the window left open.
As you get older, you tend to forget things.
Trains tend to run late in winter.
Please don't leave the water running.

blocks.s: Three more on the ます-stem:
**っこない** is a casual "no way": 分かりっこない (there's no way they'd understand).
**ようがない** means there's no way to do it: 連絡しようがない (there's no way to contact them).
**がたい** (難い) means something is hard to do emotionally, or hard to accept: 信じがたい (hard to believe).

sections.title: No way, and hard to: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: There's no way we'll make it, even if we leave now.
I don't have their number, so there's no way to contact them.
That's a hard story to believe.
There's no way a child would understand that.

blocks.s: **べき** says what ought to happen: 謝るべきだ (you should apologise). Add it to the dictionary form. する often shortens to **すべき**.

**まい** is a firm "won't" or "surely not", in writing and formal speech: 二度と行くまい (I'll never go again), 言うまい (surely he won't say it). Add it to the dictionary form. る-verbs can also drop る (食べまい), and する gives するまい or すまい.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: If you do something wrong, you should apologise straight away.
I'll never go to a shop like that again.
Promises should be kept.
He surely won't say anything more.

blocks.s: The classical negative **ぬ** survives in set phrases and writing: 知らぬ顔 (an innocent face), 帰らぬ人 (someone who has died). In speech it became **ん**: 知らん, 分からん. Add it to the old negative stem; する becomes **せぬ** / せん.

sections.title: The old negative ぬ: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: He acted as if he knew nothing.
My grandfather passed away last year.
It ended without anything being understood.

blocks.s: **げ** describes how someone looks or seems: 寂しげ (lonely-looking), 得意げ (proud-looking). い-adjectives swap い for げ; な-adjectives add it. It then works like a な-adjective: 寂しげな顔, 得意げに話す. いい becomes よさげ, a casual "looks good".
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: She had a lonely look on her face.
My little brother talked about it proudly.
There's a suspicious-looking man standing there.
This place looks good.

blocks.s: Every N2 pattern, with N2 words. Most build on the ます-stem or the old negative stem.

cards.en: It's the boss's orders, so I have no choice but to go.

blocks.s: **ねばならない** is the formal "must": the old negative stem plus ねばならない: 行かねばならない. する becomes **せねばならない**. ならぬ is even more literary.
**ずとも** means "even without": 言わずとも分かる (you understand without being told). する becomes せずとも.

sections.title: Must, formally, and even without: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: I must hurry to be on time for the appointment.
It's something you understand without being told.

lessons.title: As if about to, and in order to

sections.title: As if about to, and in order to

blocks.s: **んばかり** means "as if about to": 泣かんばかりの顔 (a face on the verge of tears), 言わんばかり (as good as saying). The old negative stem plus んばかり; する becomes せんばかり.
**べく** is a formal "in order to": 確かめるべく (in order to confirm). The dictionary form plus べく; する becomes **すべく**.
**んがため** is a literary "for the sake of": 勝たんがため (in order to win). The old negative stem plus んがため(に).

sections.title: As if about to, and in order to: in use

blocks.s: Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: She apologised, on the verge of tears.
I headed to the scene to confirm the facts.

after: はどんなことでもした。
cards.en: He did anything at all in order to win.

blocks.s: **ようものなら** means "if you were to (and it would be a disaster)": the volitional plus ものなら: 遅れようものなら (if you dare be late). The result is always something bad.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Be even a minute late and the teacher gets angry.

Dare to disagree with the manager and you'll regret it.

blocks.s: Classical Japanese adjective forms still turn up in writing, speeches and set phrases.
**かろう** is the classical "probably": い-adjectives swap い for かろう: 寒かろう (it must be cold), よかろう (that will do). な-adjectives and nouns take **であろう**.
**き** is the classical form before a noun: 高き山 (a lofty mountain), よき友 (a good friend). な-adjectives take **なる**: 静かなる夜.
Now the same forms in sentences, and the other way round: spotting which form a word is in.

cards.en: Hokkaido must be terribly cold in winter.
I've been blessed with good friends.
The moon was reflected in the still lake.
That will do.

options: classical before a noun (き / なる)
